title: The EDGE Grant Explained: How Singapore Businesses Now Fund Finance Automation After PSG
summary: PSG closed to new applications in September 2026. EDGE replaced it with a S$100,000 cap and a S$30,000 digital sub-cap. What finance teams must know.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** The Productivity Solutions Grant stopped accepting new applications at the end of September 2026. Enterprise Singapore's EDGE grant, launched 30 September 2026, replaced PSG, the Enterprise Development Grant and Market Readiness Assistance with one grant covering eight business areas and over a hundred activities. For a finance automation project the binding number is not the S$100,000 annual grant cap but the S$30,000 sub-cap on single-function digital solutions and integrated enterprise systems, which at a 50 percent support level corresponds to roughly S$60,000 of qualifying spend. Two mechanics decide whether a project funds cleanly: applications are never retrospective, so a deposit paid before submission forfeits the claim entirely, and disbursement is reimbursement-only through a single one-time claim.


## A Signed Quote and a Grant That Had Closed


In August 2026 the group financial controller of a Singapore-headquartered services company builds the internal case for accounts payable automation. Three vendor quotes, a board paper showing roughly 300 supplier invoices a month handled by two people, a projected reduction in handling time near 40 percent.


Every version of the funding model assumes the Productivity Solutions Grant: a pre-approved solution, a familiar 50 percent support level, a process the company had navigated once before.


The quote is countersigned in the first week of October. The application is opened the same week — and PSG is no longer accepting new applications. Nor is the Enterprise Development Grant. Nor is Market Readiness Assistance. All three closed to new submissions at the end of September 2026, replaced on 30 September by a single grant called EDGE.


The project is not dead. But its funding assumptions are now wrong in three specific ways: the cap is structured differently, the support rate depends on which activity the project is filed under, and the deposit the controller was about to pay would have disqualified the claim outright.


This article covers what EDGE is, who runs it, how its two caps interact, which route a finance automation project should take, and the sequence that keeps a claim payable. It does not re-explain PSG mechanics — for that, our guides to[the PSG grant for AI accounting automation](https://peakflo.co/blog/productivity-solutions-grant-ai-accounting-automation-singapore-2026) and[PSG eligibility for Singapore SMEs](https://peakflo.co/blog/psg-grant-eligibility-singapore-smes-accounting-automation) remain accurate for applications already in flight.


## Who Actually Runs the EDGE Grant?


EDGE is administered by[Enterprise Singapore](https://www.enterprisesg.gov.sg/financial-support/edge-grant) . Not by IMDA.


This needs saying plainly, because a large share of search traffic arrives looking for the “IMDA EDGE grant”, and the mistake is understandable rather than careless. The single-function digital solutions that EDGE funds are browsed through[IMDA’s SMEs Go Digital](https://www.imda.gov.sg/how-we-can-help/smes-go-digital) platform, which hosts the[pre-approved digital solutions](https://www.imda.gov.sg/how-we-can-help/smes-go-digital/pre-approved-digital-solutions) listing. A company discovers its AP software on an IMDA page, reads about its pre-approved status there, then applies for money through an Enterprise Singapore grant.


Two agencies, two roles, one project. IMDA curates and lists the solutions; Enterprise Singapore assesses the application and disburses the grant. Check solution status on the IMDA listing, but never look for the application form there. How the two platforms interact is the subject of our guide to[SMEs Go Digital for finance automation](https://peakflo.co/blog/imda-smes-go-digital-finance-automation-singapore) .


One further clarification: EDGE is not an acronym. The name is intended to convey competitive edge rather than expand into something.


## What EDGE Replaced, and What Happens to Projects Mid-Flight


EDGE consolidates three grants companies routinely confused with one another. PSG funded off-the-shelf productivity solutions. EDG funded larger transformation projects including consultancy and internal manpower. MRA funded overseas market entry. A Singapore SME digitalising finance while expanding abroad previously ran two or three applications in parallel, with different assessors and claim rules.


Previous grant What it funded Status from end-September 2026 Where it now sits in EDGE


Productivity Solutions Grant (PSG) Pre-approved off-the-shelf productivity and digital solutions Closed to new applications Automation and Digitalisation activities, including single-function digital solutions


Enterprise Development Grant (EDG) Capability-building projects, consultancy, process redesign Closed to new applications Business Strategy, Financial Management, Innovation and Standards activities


Market Readiness Assistance (MRA) Overseas market entry, promotion and business development Closed to new applications Internationalisation activities, at the higher support tier


Three points matter for anyone caught at the boundary.


**Applications submitted before the cut-off continue under their original terms.** A PSG application filed in September is assessed as a PSG application, with the support rate, cap and claim conditions in the original Letter of Offer standing.


**Ongoing projects are supported to completion.** An approved project running into 2027 is not retroactively converted to EDGE terms, and its claim process is unchanged.


**New scope requires a new application.** This is where companies get caught. Additional modules, additional entities or a second phase cannot be appended to a legacy PSG approval. They need a fresh EDGE application under the relevant activity, submitted before that new work starts.


For companies that had been weighing PSG against EDG, our[comparison of the two legacy grants](https://peakflo.co/blog/psg-grant-vs-edg-grant-accounting-automation-comparison) explains the trade-off EDGE has now collapsed into a single activity-based structure.


## Are You Eligible for the EDGE Grant?


Eligibility is close to the familiar Enterprise Singapore test, and the thresholds are specific enough to check in minutes.


- A business entity registered and operating in Singapore
- At least 30 percent local shareholding held by Singapore citizens or permanent residents
- Not a non-profit organisation, society, religious entity, voluntary welfare organisation, statutory board or government subsidiary


SME classification, which decides the support rate, requires either group annual sales turnover of no more than S$100 million or no more than 200 employees. The test is an either-or, applied at group level — a point regularly misread by groups with several Singapore-registered subsidiaries. A 60-employee Singapore entity inside a group turning over S$400 million is not an SME for this purpose.


Non-SMEs are not excluded; they receive a lower rate. For a multi-entity group that is worth modelling early, because the gap between the two rates changes the net cost of the same project materially and the group-level test may not produce the answer local management expects. Verifying registration and shareholding through[ACRA](https://www.acra.gov.sg/) records first avoids an avoidable rejection.


## The Two Caps, and Why S$30,000 Is the Number That Matters


EDGE operates two caps simultaneously, and almost every scoping mistake comes from attending to the wrong one.


The **overall annual grant cap is S$100,000 per company** . Within it sits a **S$30,000 sub-cap** covering single-function digital solutions, integrated enterprise systems and selected automation activities — counted inside the S$100,000 rather than additional to it. Both reset annually on 1 April, on a 1 April to 31 March cycle.


A finance automation project — payable, receivable, expense, payment workflow — lands squarely in the sub-capped category. So the S$100,000 figure, which is what appears in most summaries of the programme, is effectively irrelevant here. The operative ceiling is S$30,000.


Support rates differ by activity, and the nuance deserves care rather than one headline percentage. The highest-supported activities carry up to 70 percent for SMEs and 50 percent for non-SMEs, and those tiers apply to internationalisation and sustainability. The general level across most activities, including digitalisation and automation, is up to 50 percent for SMEs and 30 percent for non-SMEs. Because the rate attaches to the activity rather than the applicant, the activity you file under is a financial decision, not an administrative one.


Parameter SME Non-SME Notes


Overall annual grant cap S$100,000 S$100,000 Per company, resets 1 April


Digital and automation sub-cap S$30,000 S$30,000 Counted within the S$100,000


Support rate, general activities Up to 50% Up to 30% Includes automation and digitalisation


Support rate, highest-supported activities Up to 70% Up to 50% Internationalisation and sustainability


Qualifying spend at which sub-cap binds Around S$60,000 Around S$100,000 At the general support rate


Applications per activity One One Multiple concurrent applications permitted


That fifth row is the planning insight. For an SME at 50 percent support the sub-cap binds at roughly S$60,000 of qualifying cost. Below that, every additional dollar of scope attracts 50 cents of grant; above it, scope is entirely self-funded within that grant year. A S$55,000 project and a S$140,000 project attract the same S$30,000.


Because the caps reset on 1 April, a genuinely phased programme spanning the year boundary can draw on two sub-caps. The phasing must be real — each phase a distinct activity with its own application and claim — and driven by implementation sequencing rather than constructed for the grant. Our[AP automation ROI analysis](https://peakflo.co/blog/accounts-payable-automation-roi-analysis) covers the business case, and the[savings calculator](https://peakflo.co/savings-calculator) estimates the benefit side.


## Single-Function Solution or Integrated System?


EDGE distinguishes between a single-function digital solution and an integrated enterprise system, and the boundary is defined rather than discretionary.


Integrated enterprise system support requires a **minimum of three core functions** from a defined list: Financial Management, Supply Chain and Inventory Management, Sales and CRM, HR Management, Project Management, Asset Management, Field Service Management, Fleet Management, Manufacturing Management.


Count honestly. A deployment covering accounts payable, accounts receivable and employee expense management is substantial, but all three sit inside Financial Management. That is one core function, not three, and the project is assessed as a single-function digital solution. Adding a procurement module because it crosses into Supply Chain, when the business has no operational need for it, is the scope inflation that produces an unused module and an awkward claim.


Companies already running an integrated system often undercount in the other direction. A group implementing finance automation alongside CRM and HR in the same programme may legitimately reach three core functions, provided the implementations are genuinely integrated rather than three unrelated purchases bundled into one application.


For most finance automation projects the single-function route is both the honest answer and the faster one. Where a finance platform must coexist with a legacy ERP, the integration design matters more than the grant classification, as we discuss in our guide to[legacy ERP integration challenges](https://peakflo.co/blog/legacy-erp-integration-challenges-sap-migration) .


## Pre-Approved Versus Non-Pre-Approved Vendors: One Week or Ten


This is the most commercially consequential detail in the programme, and it is frequently misread as a question of eligibility when it is really a question of time.


A pre-approved solution has already been assessed, so the application processes in roughly **one week** . A solution that is not pre-approved requires functional assessment inside your application, which takes roughly **ten weeks** . The non-pre-approved solution remains acceptable provided it delivers the required functions for the activity. The listing is a fast lane, not a gate.


Nine weeks of difference is the real decision. For a company replacing an incumbent spend-management vendor on a contract expiring in January, ten weeks of assessment before work may commence can be flatly incompatible with the timeline — and since retrospective applications are not supported, starting early to hit the deadline forfeits the grant. For a mid-year implementation, ten weeks is an acceptable wait for the right platform.


Dimension Pre-approved solution Not pre-approved


Typical processing time Around 1 week Around 10 weeks


Eligible for support Yes Yes, if required functions are delivered


Functional assessment Already completed by the agency Performed within your application


Where to verify status IMDA SMEs Go Digital listing Confirm requirements with the agency first


Evidence burden on applicant Lower, solution already evaluated Higher, functional fit must be demonstrated


Suits projects that are Timeline-constrained or contract-driven Capability-driven with lead time available


Main risk Choosing the listed solution over the right one Underestimating the assessment window


The failure mode worth naming: picking a weaker pre-approved solution purely for the faster route, then working around its limitations for three years in exchange for a one-off S$30,000. The grant is a subsidy on a decision, not the decision itself. Where the underlying question is whether to move off a manual or legacy process at all, our analysis of[why CFOs are switching from traditional AP to AI-powered automation](https://peakflo.co/blog/cfos-switching-traditional-ap-to-ai) addresses that choice on its own merits.


## How Do You Apply Through the Business Grants Portal?


Applications go through the Business Grants Portal, which requires Corppass roles of **BGP Preparer** and **BGP Acceptor** assigned to named individuals. One application is filed per activity, and multiple concurrent applications are permitted — relevant for a company pursuing digitalisation and internationalisation activities in the same grant year.


The sequence that keeps a claim payable:


1. Assign Corppass BGP Preparer and BGP Acceptor roles. Do this first; role provisioning regularly adds days.
2. Identify the correct activity across the eight business areas, using the Enterprise Singapore listing and the BizSG recommender tool.
3. Scope the solution and apply the three-core-function test to settle classification.
4. Confirm the vendor route and build the one-week or ten-week assessment window into the project plan.
5. Submit before committing any work or payment.
6. Accept the Letter of Offer issued on approval.
7. Implement, retaining invoices and proof of payment contemporaneously.
8. Submit the single claim after completion and full payment.


Where management consultancy forms part of the project, activities in that category prefer consultants certified to SS 680. Confirm certification status before scoping, since substituting a consultant after approval is considerably harder than selecting the right one initially; professional bodies such as[ISCA](https://isca.org.sg/) are a reasonable starting point. The portal mechanics are deliberately similar to the legacy process, so our[step-by-step PSG application guide](https://peakflo.co/blog/how-to-apply-psg-grant-accounting-automation-step-by-step-2026) remains a useful reference for the portal itself, allowing for the change of grant.


## The Retrospective Application Trap


**Retrospective applications are not supported.** Any work commenced or any payment made before the application is submitted disqualifies the claim.


This is the most common and most costly mistake under the programme, and it is almost always made in good faith by a competent team. The pattern recurs:


- A deposit is paid to hold implementation capacity before the application goes in
- A proof of concept runs “to validate the solution first”, using vendor time that forms part of the quoted scope
- Configuration begins on a verbal agreement while the paperwork catches up
- A subscription starts on the first of the month because that is when billing begins


Each commits the company before submission, and each forfeits the grant on a project that would otherwise have qualified comfortably. There is no appeal on the grounds that the work was minor or the payment refundable.


The discipline is unglamorous: nothing is signed, paid or started until the application is in. That means telling the vendor the start date depends on a grant outcome — a straightforward conversation to have early and a difficult one after a deposit has cleared. On a ten-week route it also means the project plan must absorb the wait rather than quietly beginning work during it.


## How the Money Arrives: Reimbursement and the One-Claim Rule


EDGE is disbursed on a **reimbursement basis** . There is no cash advance. The company funds the whole project from working capital, and the claim follows completion and full payment. For a S$60,000 project at 50 percent support, the company pays S$60,000 and later recovers S$30,000. Cash flow modelling should treat the grant as a subsequent inflow, not a discount on the invoice.


Three mechanics then govern the claim.


**One-time claim submission only.** Additional claims against the same project are rejected, and qualifying cost omitted from that single submission is forfeited.


**One extension of the claim due date is permitted.** Given the one-shot rule, taking the extension and submitting complete documentation beats submitting on time and incomplete.


**A Letter of Offer is issued on approval.** It sets out approved cost, support level and claim conditions, and acceptance is what authorises the project to begin. Read those conditions at acceptance rather than at claim time, because the evidence they require must be collected during implementation. Companies that held SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit should also note that its final claims deadline was 30 November 2026.


Qualifying project cost Grant at 50% SME rate Effect of S$30,000 sub-cap Grant received Effective support


S$20,000 S$10,000 Not reached S$10,000 50%


S$40,000 S$20,000 Not reached S$20,000 50%


S$60,000 S$30,000 Exactly at the sub-cap S$30,000 50%


S$90,000 S$45,000 Capped S$30,000 33%


S$150,000 S$75,000 Capped S$30,000 20%


The bands above use illustrative industry cost ranges for a multi-entity finance automation project — subscription, implementation, data migration and training — rather than any vendor’s pricing. The pattern holds regardless: the first S$60,000 of scope is half-funded and everything beyond it is not. A group implementing across many entities should expect the sub-cap to bind, and should plan the self-funded portion deliberately rather than discovering it at claim time.

## Our Verdict: Is EDGE Worth Building a Project Around?


Having worked through the programme’s structure, our assessment is that EDGE reduces administrative load for most Singapore companies, but changes the shape of the funding available for finance automation in one way worth understanding first.


The simplification is real: one portal, one activity taxonomy, one claim process, rather than three grants with different rules that companies routinely applied to in parallel.


The change in shape is the sub-cap. A S$30,000 ceiling on digital and automation activities means EDGE meaningfully funds a focused deployment and only partially funds a large multi-entity programme. That is defensible policy design, and no reason to shrink a project justified on its own merits.


### Prioritise this if


- You are Singapore-registered with at least 30 percent local shareholding and a project already justified without a grant
- Qualifying cost is at or below roughly S$60,000, where the full support rate applies
- Your preferred solution appears on the IMDA pre-approved listing, giving a one-week route
- You have not yet signed, paid or started anything
- The project can be phased genuinely across the 1 April grant year boundary
- You can fund the full cost from working capital and wait for reimbursement


### Deprioritise this if


- Work has already commenced or a deposit has been paid, so the claim is disqualified
- Group turnover or headcount places you outside the SME band and the lower rate changes the case materially
- The project is large enough that S$30,000 is immaterial to the decision
- Cash flow cannot absorb the full cost ahead of reimbursement
- Your timeline cannot accommodate ten weeks and the only suitable solution is not pre-approved


**Our recommendation:** treat EDGE as a subsidy on a decision already made correctly, and protect the two mechanics that determine whether the money arrives. Submit before committing anything at all, and prepare a single complete claim rather than a timely incomplete one. Those disciplines are worth more than any optimisation of scope or activity selection, because they separate a funded project from an identical one paying full price. Choose the right platform first, then find the activity that fits it — never the reverse.


## Conclusion: The Grant Changed, the Discipline Did Not


The transition from PSG to EDGE is a consolidation, not a withdrawal. Support for finance automation remains substantial, the eligibility test is broadly unchanged, and the process is simpler than running separate PSG, EDG and MRA applications ever was.


What has changed is which numbers to plan against. The S$100,000 annual cap is not the relevant figure for a finance automation project; the S$30,000 sub-cap is, and at the general support level it binds at around S$60,000 of qualifying spend. The rate attaches to the activity rather than the company, so activity selection carries real financial weight. And the vendor route decides whether assessment takes one week or ten, which for a contract-driven replacement can matter more than the grant itself.


For the controller in October 2026 with a countersigned quote, the answer is unchanged in substance and entirely changed in detail. The project still qualifies. The route is now EDGE rather than PSG, the ceiling is S$30,000 rather than whatever the old model assumed, and the deposit must wait until the application is in. That last point is the one that would have cost the grant, and the one that costs other companies theirs every month.


## Frequently Asked Questions


**Is the EDGE grant run by IMDA or Enterprise Singapore?**


Enterprise Singapore administers the EDGE grant. The confusion arises because the single-function digital solutions that EDGE funds are browsed through IMDA’s SMEs Go Digital platform, which hosts the pre-approved digital solutions listing. So companies discover the software on an IMDA page and then apply for funding through an Enterprise Singapore grant, which is why the term IMDA EDGE grant circulates widely.


**Has the Productivity Solutions Grant been discontinued?**


Yes, for new applications. PSG stopped accepting new applications at the end of September 2026, as did the Enterprise Development Grant and Market Readiness Assistance. EDGE launched on 30 September 2026 and consolidates all three. Applications already submitted before the cut-off continue to be assessed under their original terms, and approved projects already running are supported through to completion.


**What happens to a PSG project that is already mid-flight?**


It continues under PSG terms. The support rate, cap and claim conditions in the original Letter of Offer remain binding, and the project is supported to completion. What changes is that any new, additional scope cannot be bolted on to the old application. New scope requires a fresh EDGE application, and it must be submitted before that new work begins.


**How much funding is available for finance automation under EDGE?**


Support levels differ by activity. The general level across most activities is up to 50 percent of qualifying cost for SMEs and up to 30 percent for non-SMEs, with higher tiers of up to 70 percent for SMEs and 50 percent for non-SMEs applying to internationalisation and sustainability activities. Finance automation normally sits in the general band, subject to a S$30,000 sub-cap.


**Why does the S$30,000 sub-cap matter more than the S$100,000 cap?**


Because the sub-cap is the constraint a finance automation project actually hits. The overall annual grant cap is S$100,000 per company, but single-function digital solutions, integrated enterprise systems and selected automation activities carry a S$30,000 sub-cap counted within that S$100,000. At a 50 percent support rate, S$30,000 of grant corresponds to S$60,000 of qualifying spend.


**Who is eligible for the EDGE grant?**


A business entity registered and operating in Singapore with at least 30 percent local shareholding held by Singapore citizens or permanent residents. Non-profit organisations, societies, religious entities, voluntary welfare organisations, statutory boards and government subsidiaries are excluded. SME classification requires group annual sales turnover of no more than S$100 million or no more than 200 employees.


**Can I use a vendor that is not on the pre-approved list?**


Yes. A solution that is not pre-approved remains acceptable provided it delivers the required functions for the activity. The difference is processing time rather than permission. Pre-approved vendors are assessed in roughly one week because the solution has already been evaluated, whereas a non-pre-approved solution takes around ten weeks because the functional assessment happens inside your application.


**What counts as an integrated enterprise system under EDGE?**


A system covering a minimum of three core functions from a defined list that includes Financial Management, Supply Chain and Inventory Management, Sales and CRM, HR Management, Project Management, Asset Management, Field Service Management, Fleet Management and Manufacturing Management. Fewer than three core functions means the deployment is assessed as a single-function digital solution instead, which is a different activity with its own terms.


**Can I apply for EDGE after work on the project has started?**


No. Retrospective applications are not supported. Any work commenced or any payment made before the application is submitted disqualifies the claim. This includes deposits, pilot fees and configuration work begun on a handshake. The application must be submitted and the outcome known before the company commits either effort or money to the project.


**When does the grant money actually arrive?**


After the project is complete and fully paid for. EDGE is disbursed on a reimbursement basis with no cash advance, so the company funds the entire project from its own working capital first, then submits a claim. Finance teams should model the grant as a later cash inflow rather than a reduction in the invoice they have to settle.


**How many claims can I submit for one project?**


One. Claim submission is a one-time event and additional claims against the same project are rejected. If part of the qualifying cost is omitted from that single submission, it is forfeited. One extension of the claim due date is permitted, which makes waiting for complete documentation preferable to submitting an incomplete claim on time.


**Do the EDGE caps reset every year?**


Yes, annually on 1 April, running on a 1 April to 31 March cycle. That makes the grant year a planning variable rather than a technicality, because a project scoped in two phases across a year boundary can draw on two separate S$30,000 sub-caps. The phasing has to be genuine, with each phase a distinct activity and application.
